sections.title: Learning like flash cards
paragraphs: If you have ever studied with flash cards, you already understand the core idea behind most machine learning. You look at the front of the card, try to remember the back, and check yourself. Do that enough times and patterns start to stick.

Most machine learning you will use day to day is {{supervisedLearning}}. That means we show a {{model}} many examples where the correct answer is already known, and the {{model}} learns to predict that answer for new inputs.

Each example has two parts. The {{input}} is what you show the {{model}} — a photo, a customer email, two numbers in a puzzle, or a prompt. The {{target}} is the answer you want it to learn — spam or not spam, dog or cat, the correct sum, or a helpful reply.

Training is repeated practice. The {{model}} makes a {{prediction}}, compares it to the {{target}}, and adjusts internal numbers called {{weights}} so the next {{prediction}} is closer. You do not program every rule by hand; the examples teach the pattern.
This is different from dumping raw files into a folder and hoping something happens. {{supervisedLearning}} needs {{labeledData}} — inputs with agreed correct answers a human expert could defend.
bullets: {{target}} — the correct answer for that input.
{{prediction}} — what the {{model}} outputs before it has learned well.

check.prompt: A teammate says: "We downloaded 50,000 product photos with no tags — we can train a {{classifier}} tomorrow." What is the honest reply?
check.answer: We still need labels — photos alone are not supervised examples.
choices: Yes — more photos always means a better model.
We still need labels — photos alone are not supervised examples.
No — supervised learning only works on text.
Yes — the model can invent its own labels during training.
check.explanation: A {{classifier}} needs {{labeledData}}: each photo needs a {{target}} such as product category or defect type. Without labels there is nothing to grade {{prediction}}s against, so training cannot start.

sections.title: See inputs paired with targets
paragraphs: Every training row is a pair: an {{input}} and a {{target}}. The {{model}} never magically knows the right answer — it only learns because we show pairs over and over.

The pairs can look very different depending on the task. A routing {{model}} might map a user message to an intent. A vision {{model}} might map pixels to a category. A small neural network in the next lab maps two numbers to one output.
Click each row below to see the {{target}} for that {{input}}. Notice how different the tasks look while the pattern stays the same: show input, teach target.

reveals.reveal: Intent: account_recovery — the {{model}} should route this to the password-reset flow.

reveals.prompt: Input: Photo of a golden retriever → Target: ?
reveals.reveal: Label: dog — the {{model}} should classify the image as a dog.

reveals.prompt: Input: (0, 0) and (1, 1) in an XOR puzzle → Target: ?
reveals.reveal: 0 for both corners, 1 for (0,1) and (1,0) — you will train exactly this in the neural network lab.

check.prompt: You want a {{model}} to score essay quality from 1–5. Which dataset fits {{supervisedLearning}} best?
choices: Essays with no scores — only word counts
Random paragraphs scraped from the web
check.explanation: {{supervisedLearning}} needs a {{target}} for every {{input}}. Human 1–5 ratings are the {{target}}; essays alone are only half of each example.

sections.title: What counts — and what does not
paragraphs: Not every dataset can train a supervised {{model}}. The rule is simple: for each {{input}}, experts should be able to agree on the right {{target}}.
Good examples include customer reviews with star ratings, code snippets labeled pass or fail, medical images with diagnoses, and prompt–answer pairs edited by humans for quality.
Weak examples include a folder of images with no tags, text with no agreed label, or the same prompt answered differently by every reviewer with no rubric.
In AiEval you will later compare model answers to the same prompt. That only works when you can define what "better" means — another form of {{target}}.
Next up: **What is a dataset?** — how labeled rows form a {{dataset}}, and why the lab offers puzzles like AND and XOR.
bullets: Does not count: unlabeled piles of raw data.
Rule of thumb: if experts can agree on the answer, you can build an example.

check.prompt: In one short phrase: what two things must every supervised training example include?
accept: an input and a target label
check.explanation: Supervised learning is learning from pairs. Without both an {{input}} and a {{target}}, the {{model}} has nothing to practice on and nothing to grade {{prediction}}s against.

recapQuestions.prompt: Which situation is LEAST compatible with {{supervisedLearning}}?
recapQuestions.answer: Millions of web pages with no quality scores or labels
choices: 10,000 emails labeled spam or not spam
Millions of web pages with no quality scores or labels
Images of skin lesions with doctor diagnoses
recapQuestions.explanation: Unlabeled web pages lack {{target}}s. The other options all pair {{input}}s with agreed {{target}}s — exactly what {{supervisedLearning}} needs.

recapQuestions.prompt: Why do we show a {{model}} the {{target}} during training?
recapQuestions.answer: So it can compare predictions to the correct answer and improve
choices: So it can compare predictions to the correct answer and improve
So it can hide the target from users at runtime
So we never need a test set
So the model can skip making predictions
recapQuestions.explanation: Training is feedback. The {{model}} predicts, sees the {{target}}, measures error, and updates {{weights}}. Without the {{target}}, there is no signal for improvement.
